title: Fade
description: A lane in Cinque Terre seen from the cobbles, looking straight up between painted houses into a summer sky, and the thirty years of sun that come after it. Drag forward and every wall ages by the light it actually receives: the top floors, open to the whole sky, bleach and chalk first, while the low storeys, which see only the slot of sky between the eaves, keep their colour longest. The pink and orange walls turned to the sun go to pale plaster within a generation (the pink top floor to a dusty rose); the coral wall across the lane faces north, sees only its slot of sky, and keeps its red. While the clock moves, the year's suns run across the walls again as light and shade, the slot's shadow line and the shutters' and lanterns' shapes passing over the facades, and the fade builds up behind the light; at rest the light goes back to the photograph and the faded paint stays.
intent: Reality pieces, technique 8 (Fade): manipulate a real photograph physically. One photograph is baked into an annual solar dose per pixel (MoGe-2 metric point map; world up recovered from the facades' vertical faces, the lane's orientation from the photo's own sun fitted on the walls' shading one paint colour at a time; 144 sun directions over a year at 44 N, each tested first against the rooflines across the lane as clean geometry (the sky mask's edge on the coral wall and on the roofs at the end of the lane split into straight runs by RANSAC, each lifted to a level 3D line at the height MoGe's points under it agree on, the coral's eave opposite the pink set along the lane at the lane's width from the corner where its roofline turns, and each extruded as its facade down to the lane plus a half-metre eave), then with a screen-space depth-march visibility test against the houses, which takes no hit along those skylines where MoGe's depth blurs into the sky, clear-sky beam x the Ligurian coast's sunshine fraction, plus sky-view factor x diffuse, at 1/4 resolution on CPU; then the thin things that have hung there for decades, SAM masks of the open shutter leaves, lanterns, bracket and gelato sign plus black-hat lines for the drying lines, hooks and rods, stood off their walls and marched again at 1/2 resolution along 72 suns over the year and over each wall pixel's sky, so each takes the share of the sun's path it covers: a shutter leaf or a lantern leaves a firm tan of unfaded paint, a drying cord whose shadow sweeps the wall through the day only a faint trace), then, because the frame holds almost none of the low storeys across the lane, the far wall put back analytically from each pixel's height above the lane (the slot of sky), the sky graded live as if through a polariser on MoGe-2's sky mask (clear sky re-shot as a cyan-cobalt that deepens to the zenith at the frame's centre, cloud keeping its own light), the photo's own illumination (to recover albedo), and a SAM mask of the one bare stone wall. Live, the dose is put on a power curve (paint holds, then fails), albedo becomes optical density, split into carbon black and cyan / magenta / yellow pigment, each fading exponentially with dose after an induction that holds a sunlit wall for its first few years (the orange face under its eave for five or so), with the clock set so the sunlit faces have reached their end colours by year thirty (yellow and magenta about 4x faster than cyan, their differential capped so a coat turns its hue by no more than a few degrees), plus a thin skin of yellow and magenta lost to the diffuse sky alone, linear in the dose with no induction, so the north-facing coral wall gives up a twentieth or so of its chroma and keeps its red (near #963E31) without looking frozen; and the lime render chalks toward a lime white (#EEE8DD) over a residual tint of about half its own paint's chroma (never less than a visible tint), so a sunlit pink wall settles at a dusty pink (near #E9CFC6, its tint turning from salmon toward rose as its ochre's yellow goes first, and chalking nearer the lime, having so little pigment) and an orange one at a pale apricot (near #EBCB9E), not one cream. And the cause is shown while the clock moves: the same 144 suns, in order (each month's day forward then back, so the sun never jumps; once over the thirty years), are marched live in the shader at half resolution against the fitted rooflines, the bake's depth, normals, the occluders' slabs and the analytic far wall where the frame shows none of it (geo.webp, slab.webp), and brought up to the plate by a depth- and normal-guided joint bilateral filter whose width is the penumbra the sun's 0.53 degree disc throws from the blocker each ray hit (an eave's line crisp under it, a roof across the lane's soft), and shown as light on the faded albedo, not a grade: albedo x (the lane's sky + a near-neutral sun x visibility x N.L), the beam's cosine taken softly (a lit render scatters), about a stop between sun and shade, so a lit wall keeps its paint's own hue and grain; each pixel's years then follow the clock quickly where that sun stands on it and slowly in its shade, so the fade builds up behind the light, and at rest the light settles back to the photograph and every pixel takes the clock's years. A still with a sun held (?years=18&sun=104, an equinox afternoon, when the coral house's eave across the lane cuts one straight line across the pink wall, level on it like its own courses) is the clock caught mid-drag: the walls in that sun are at the clock's years, those in its shade hardly started, so chalked dusty rose sits against the photograph's saturated salmon along the shadow line: the eave's line is taken where each pixel's ray meets the pink wall's fitted plane (MoGe's depth ripples by a hand or two), so it is straight and level, and its penumbra is drawn across the line only, crisp. On old painted signs 'only the blue remains': https://www.maru-sin.co.jp/en/news_sanpo/january-2023_01/ ; yellow and magenta process inks are the least lightfast: https://printing.org/content/2018/03/28/a-customer-has-complained-that-a-poster-is-fading-almost-immediately-with-exposure-to
sources: Photograph: 'Low angle view of colorful Mediterranean buildings surrounding a bright blue sky' by Victor Rosario (https://unsplash.com/@victor_rosario) on Unsplash, Unsplash License (https://unsplash.com/license). https://unsplash.com/photos/colorful-mediterranean-buildings-under-blue-sky-9rFrYPdisXU (file: https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1787152171273-de25142325a1, 6192x4128, Sony ILCE-6700, Cinque Terre). Cropped to 4:3 (columns 200 to 5704), resampled to 2000x1500. Normals, metric depth and sky by MoGe-2 (tools/depth/normals.py); the stone wall's mask and the thin occluders' masks by SAM 2.1 (tools/depth/segment.py); maps baked by tools/depth/bakes/fade (prep.py, dose.py, roofs.py, canyon.py, mat.py, render.py, sweep.py) into plate.webp, light.webp, mat.webp, render.webp, geo.webp and slab.webp.
